UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                             )          Docket No. ER26-3515-000

         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO REPLY AND REPLY COMMENTS OF
          AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER SERVICE CORPORATION

       American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf of its affiliates

Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power

Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, and Wheeling Power

Company (collectively, “AEP”), submits this motion for leave to reply and reply. AEP

seeks leave to reply to several comments submitted in response to PJM Interconnection,

LLC’s (“PJM’s”) proposed tariff revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“PJM Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities

(“RAA”) proposed in the above-captioned docket to establish Interim Resource Adequacy

Service (“IRAS”) effective October 12, 2026.1 AEP also seeks leave to reply to PJM’s

Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer filed on September 23, 2026.2 As AEP discusses

below, PJM’s treatment of the Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) Alternative under its

IRAS proposal, as clarified by AEP’s comments in this proceeding, is necessary to ensure




1
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Res. Adequacy
Serv. and a Large Load Registry to Address Sys. Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515 (filed Aug. 13, 2026)
(“IRAS Proposal”).
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Morion For Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,
Docket No. ER26-3515 (filed Sept. 23, 2026) (“PJM Reply”).


                                                   1
 that the FRR Alternative remains viable and just and reasonable.3                  Critically, the

clarifications that AEP seeks from the Commission in its comments are also important to

the viability of the FRR Alternative and do not seek to avoid the requirement to serve new

Large Load with new capacity.

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO REPLY

          While Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure does

not generally permit answers to protests, the Commission has permitted answers where the

answer clarifies the issues or assists in creating a complete record. 4 Accordingly, AEP

respectfully requests leave to reply to the relevant protests and, to the extent necessary, the

relevant comments in the above-captioned docket. In several instances, the protests

misrepresent or ignore the plain language of the IRAS Proposal and how the FRR

Alternative will be addressed in the IRAS Proposal. Good cause exists to grant this motion

for leave to answer because the answer corrects those unsupported misstatements and

misrepresentations, leading to a full and complete record in this proceeding.

II.       REPLY

          A.      FRR Entities and RPM Entities Are Not Similarly Situated, and the
                  IRAS Proposal’s Differential Treatment Is Therefore Just and
                  Reasonable.

          Certain commenters argue that the IRAS Proposal is unduly preferential and

discriminatory because FRR Entities are exempt from IRAS while load serving entities



3
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments and Request for Clarification of Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp.,
Docket No. ER26-3515 (filed Sept. 3, 2026) (“AEP Comments”).
4
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2026).


                                                 2
 (“LSEs”) participating in the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) are subject to it. These

arguments fail because they rest on the flawed premise that FRR load is similarly situated

to RPM load. It is not. The critical distinction is structural: RPM Entities may rely on the

RPM auction as a backstop to meet their capacity obligations, whereas FRR Entities

cannot. Instead, FRR load can come online only if it is served by capacity that the FRR

Entity has contracted for or owns. This fundamental difference in capacity obligation

design dooms the claims of undue discrimination or preferential treatment, because the

Commission has long held that there is no undue discrimination when entities are

differently situated.5 Moreover, even if FRR Entities and RPM Entities were similarly

situated—which they are not—PJM has articulated a sound basis for the differential

treatment, and the Commission has confirmed that “there is no undue discrimination or

preference [when] we have identified appropriate reasons for it.”6 Thus, the Commission

should reject commenters’ discrimination arguments.

          East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.’s (“EKPC”) arguments exemplify this

flawed reasoning. EKPC argues that the IRAS Proposal is unduly discriminatory because

FRR Entities are exempt from IRAS while RPM Entities that have prudently planned


5
  City of Anaheim, Opinion No. 483, 113 FERC ¶ 61,091, at P 130 (2005) (“Discrimination is undue when
there is a difference in rates or services among similarly situated customers that is not justified by some
legitimate factor.”) (citations omitted); PacifiCorp Elec. Operations, 54 FERC ¶ 61,296, at 61,855
(“[U]ndue discrimination can occur only when two similarly situated customers are treated differently, and
there is no justification for the differing treatment.”) (citations omitted), reh’g denied, 55 FERC ¶ 61,461
(1991); Puget Sound Energy, Inc. v. All Jurisdictional Sellers of Energy, Opinion No. 537, 151 FERC ¶
61,173, at P 43, n.105 (2015) (quoting Energy Transfer, 120 FERC ¶ 61,086, at P 169 (2007)), rev’d on
other grounds, 157 FERC ¶ 61,026 (2016) (“It is well established that a finding of undue discrimination
requires a showing that ‘(1) two classes of customers are treated differently; and (2) the two classes of
customers are similarly situated.’”).
6
    Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 155 FERC ¶ 61,082 at P 31 (2016).


                                                     3
 capacity to serve their load remain subject to it.7 EKPC contends that, because both have

planned capacity, FRR Entities and such RPM Entities are similarly situated. 8 This

contention is wrong. The question is not whether an entity has prudently planned capacity.

Rather, the question is whether an entity has a guaranteed safety net in the RPM auction if

its capacity position proves inadequate. FRR Entities do not have that safety net, while

RPM Entities do. Thus, they are not similarly situated. The structural difference also

determines whether the entity contributes to the RPM auction shortfall that IRAS is

designed to address.

           The FRR Alternative imposes stringent self-supply obligations that distinguish FRR

Entities from RPM Entities. An FRR Entity must identify the load it expects to serve and

must own, build, or contract for the capacity necessary to serve that load in each delivery

year.9 Critically, the FRR Entity must procure sufficient capacity to serve not only

anticipated load but also any actual load that materializes during the Delivery Year.10 If

the FRR Entity’s forecast proves wrong, it has no safety net because it cannot turn to the

RPM auction for additional capacity.11

           RPM Entities face no comparable constraint. They are not required to own or

contract for their own capacity. Instead, they may rely entirely on the RPM auction to



7
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Limited Protest of East Ky. Power Coop., Inc., Docket No. ER26-3515, at
13 (filed Sept. 3, 2026) (“EKPC Comments”).
8
     EKPC Comments at Attach. 1, Affidavit of Marc Montalvo at ¶¶ 40-41.
9
    See PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff, Attach. DD, section 1.
10
     Id.
11
     PJM Reliability Assurance Agreement, Schedule 8.1, section D.1.1.


                                                     4
 satisfy their capacity obligations.12 And even if an RPM Entity chooses to self-supply, the

RPM auction remains available as a backstop if its capacity needs change. 13 This access

to the RPM auction is material to the IRAS Proposal because the RPM auction has

experienced capacity shortfalls for upcoming delivery years. These shortfalls prompted

PJM to propose IRAS. Because FRR Entities do not participate in the RPM auction and

cannot draw on it as a backstop, it is logical to exclude them from the IRAS Proposal. The

Commission should therefore reject claims that the IRAS Proposal’s differential treatment

of FRR Entities and RPM Entities is unduly discriminatory or preferential.

           Commenters also contend that it is unduly preferential and discriminatory to permit

FRR Entities to serve New Large Load using Existing Generation Capacity Resources

while RPM Entities cannot.14 This argument, too, ignores the structural differences

between the FRR Alternative and RPM. As noted above, unlike RPM Entities, which can

satisfy capacity obligations through the auction, FRR Entities must own or contract for all

the capacity needed to serve their loads. Allowing FRR Entities limited flexibility to

deploy Existing Generation Capacity Resources for New Large Load recognizes that

inflexibility in FRR Plan structuring could undermine the viability of the FRR Alternative

altogether because it has no backstop or safety net.




12
     PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff, Attach. DD, section 6.
13
     Id.
14
   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of the Elec. Power Supply Assn., Docket No. ER26-3515, at 12
(filed Sept. 3, 2026) (“EPSA Comments”).


                                                    5
           At the same time, the IRAS Proposal does not give FRR Entities unlimited

flexibility. Recognizing that FRR Entities could otherwise draw Existing Generation

Capacity Resources away from the RPM auction and exacerbate the capacity shortfall that

IRAS seeks to remedy, the IRAS Proposal imposes limitations on FRR Entities. An FRR

Entity may use Existing Generation Capacity Resources to serve New Large Load only if

the FRR Entity owned or contracted for those resources before June 1, 2027. 15 The June

1, 2027 cutoff serves dual purposes. First, it preserves the operational flexibility that FRR

Entities need to structure their FRR Plans. Second, it protects the RPM auction by

preventing FRR Entities from acquiring additional Existing Generation Capacity

Resources after the cutoff date to serve New Large Load and ensures that the IRAS

Proposal’s goal of addressing RPM auction shortfalls is not undermined by capacity

migration to FRR service.16 Again, these arguments that IRAS is unduly discriminatory or

results in preferential treatment fail and should be rejected.

          B.      The Commission Should Reject PJM’s Claims That AEP’s Proposed
                  Clarifications Will Allow It to Avoid The Requirement to Serve New
                  Large Load With New Capacity.

          In its comments, AEP requests that the Commission clarify that, when the IRAS

rules are lifted in times where capacity is not short, the FRR restrictions are similarly

lifted.17 AEP also requests that the Commission clarify that when IRAS reactivates after



15
   IRAS Proposal, Attach. B, Revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and Resource
Adequacy Agreement, Schedule 8.1, section D.1.1, Docket No. ER26-3515 (filed Aug. 13, 2026)
(“Proposed RAA”).
16
     PJM Transmittal Letter at 73-74.
17
     AEP Comments at section IV.A.


                                              6
 being dormant, FRR Entities be provided flexibility to serve any Large Loads that came

online prior to that reactivation with Existing Generation Capacity Resources. 18 As

discussed above, this flexibility is critical to ensuring that FRR Entities can economically

and reliably serve all FRR loads and recognizes the structural differences between FRR

Entities and RPM Entities.

           In response, PJM contends that these clarifications would “undermine the

overarching policy driving IRAS and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge” because the

clarifications would not result in FRR Entities serving new Large Load with new

capacity.19 PJM’s response mischaracterizes how FRR works. As PJM itself admits later

in its answer, “[b]y definition, FRR Entities must bring new capacity for all new loads

within their territory.”20 This obligation is embedded in an FRR entity’s overall obligation

to include sufficient capacity in its FRR Capacity Plan for all of its load. 21 Thus, by

definition any new Large Load served by an FRR Entity must be served by new capacity

consistent with the policy driving IRAS and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.            The

clarification AEP seeks is necessary to ensure that it has the flexibility to acquire and use

that capacity, once brought online to serve all load when the IRAS takes effect on June 1,

2027, in the most efficient manner to address overall FRR needs in future years. This is

critical to ensure that AEP can reliably and cost-effectively serve its customers.



18
     Id. at section III.B.
19
     PJM Reply at 62.
20
     Id. at 63 (citing RAA, Article 1) (emphasis in the original).
21
     Id. at 63 & n.227 (citing RAA, Schedule 8.1D, section 7).


                                                        7
 Accordingly, the Commission should reject PJM’s claim and grant the clarifications sought

by AEP in its comments.

           C.    The IRAS Proposal Should Incentivize Alignment with Its Stated Goals
                 and Avoid Jurisdictional Vulnerability.

           AEP supports commenters who argue the Commission should ensure IRAS

incentivizes actions that align with the service’s goals and that the tariff changes are legally

durable. For example, IRAS aims to address capacity shortfall in the RPM auction by

requiring RPM Entities to Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) for Eligible New

Large Load, but commenters argue that the proposal leaves it uncertain whether BYONC

will allow Eligible New Large Load to avoid being curtailed under IRAS. 22 Commenters

argue that the IRAS Proposal is structured in a way that leaves open the possibility that

Eligible New Large Load could be curtailed under IRAS even if such load has BYONC.23

Thus, AEP encourages the Commission to address any incentive misalignment present in

the IRAS Proposal.

           Commenters also highlight aspects of the IRAS Proposal that risk succumbing to

legal challenge. They note that PJM’s proposal attempts to thread the needle between state

and federal jurisdiction, but this narrow path to “cooperative federalism” is vulnerable to

challenge.24 Unlike recent large load tariff reforms that PJM claims are analogous to IRAS,

  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of Google LLC, Docket No. ER26-3515, at 1-2, 3-7 (filed Sept. 3,
2026) (“Google Comments”).
23
     Id.

Comments”).


                                                  8
 such as SPP’s HILLGA proposal and MISO’s ERAS proposal, these commenters argue

that the IRAS Proposal attempts to reach retail customers, beyond the bounds of federal

jurisdiction.25 AEP urges the Commission to require PJM to address this jurisdictional

risk. The Commission should not approve a version of the IRAS Proposal that could lead

to lengthy litigation and may very well be successfully challenged—this would contravene

the goals of IRAS to expeditiously address an urgent capacity shortfall.

          D.     Any Suggestion That AEP’s Ohio Large Load Tariff Is Not Protecting
                 Retail Customers Is Unfounded.

          Finally, the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”) contends that AEP’s

state large load tariff in Ohio26 “does not adequately protect consumers from the federal

curtailments PJM is proposing for large load customers” under IRAS.27 To the extent OCC

suggests that AEP’s Ohio large load tariff fails to protect Ohio retail customers, its assertion

is unfounded. The AEP Ohio large load tariff was approved by the Public Utilities

Commission of Ohio and is designed to recognize the importance of large loads and to

ensure they can connect and be served while protecting retail customers from unnecessary

cost increases. OCC provides no evidence that the AEP Ohio large load tariff is not

working as intended. Any suggestion otherwise is misleading.

                                                   9
 III.   CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, AEP respectfully requests that the Commission: (1)

reject commenters’ claims that the IRAS Proposal’s treatment of FRR Entities is unduly

discriminatory or preferential because FRR Entities are not similarly situated to RPM

Entities (2) reject PJM’s claims that the clarification sought by AEP will allow it to avoid

the proposed requirement to serve new Large Load with new capacity; and (3) ensure the

IRAS Proposal is legally durable and incentivizes actions that align with its stated goals.
